newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Corruption panel tells Arafat to put house in order.
newsitem.headline: Corruption panel tells Arafat to put house in order.

text.p: A committee appointed by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to investigate corruption recommended on Monday he put his house in order and that some senior officials be put on trial.

"We have discovered some serious shortcomings and there are people who are involved who should be put on trial," said Tayeb Abdel-Rahim, head of the presidential committee on corruption which submitted a 127-page report to Arafat.

He told Reuters that Arafat promised to take "immediate, firm action" in line with the recommendations. The report was not made public. Nor were any of the names disclosed. Arafat himself was not under investigation.
But Majid al-Muzainy, a committee member and judge of the high justice court, said a cabinet reshuffle was expected soon after Arafat studied the committee recommendations.

Abdel-Rahim said the committee, set up by Arafat in June, spent 300 hours investigating the conclusions of an official auditor's report which found that members of the ruling Palestinian Authority had squandered $326 million in public funds last year.

"There is no squandering of money, but we have found serious financial, legal and administrative violations and flaws, some resulting from lack of experience," Abdel-Rahim said. "We have recommended immediate stringent reforms in all these fields."
Once having signed a peace deal with Israel in 1993, Arafat shed his guerrilla image, returned to Gaza the next year and began setting up institutions of his new Palestinian Authority.
The findings of the presidential committee could improve the Authority's credibility with international donor states which pledged millions of dollars in aid to the ailing Palestinian economy.
Donors had insisted the Authority be held accountable for the money it received.

Abdel-Rahim said the committee questioned ministers, directors-general and other senior and junior Palestinian Authority officials. But he refused to say which officials should be questioned, removed from office or tried.
Muzainy said some senior officials were among those criticised.
"(There were) ministers, deputies, and others, and we suggested some measures that will satisfy all the people," he told reporters.

Palestinian lawmakers and citizens had accused Authority officials of corruption and misuse of taxpayers' money. They charged that while unemployment was skyrocketing in self-ruled areas, some ministers were building luxurious houses and owned several late-model cars and ran up huge phone bills at the Authority's expense.
Palestinians complained of bureaucracy and favouritism and padding of payrolls with employees who did little work.

"We have recommended that the Authority start swiftly to structure ministries and to set up strong auditing systems, to continue drafting laws to organise the Authority's work and to control the work of public-owned organisations," Abdel-Rahim said.
"There have been cases of serious violations which could be punished by law."
An opinion poll in June showed that most Palestinians would support an initiative by lawmakers to bring down Arafat's government over corruption.
PLO officials said Arafat himself was never accused of corruption since he lives modestly, but they said he had traditionally chosen to close his eyes to the corruption of some people around him.
